text: Everything in this course so far has run from a local CLI against a backend you configured yourself — your own credentials, your own machine doing the actual plan and apply work. Terraform Cloud is HashiCorp's own managed service that takes several of those jobs off your plate entirely, and it's worth understanding even if your own project never uses it.

A cloud block inside terraform {} replaces a backend block entirely — state storage becomes Terraform Cloud's problem, with no storage account or S3 bucket to provision and secure yourself. More importantly, it can run plan and apply remotely, on HashiCorp's own infrastructure instead of your laptop. A Terraform Cloud workspace, a different concept from the terraform workspace command in Lesson 17, connects to a VCS repo and kicks off a run on push or pull request.

The concrete thing this adds that plain Terraform doesn't have built in is a real review-before-apply workflow: a web UI shows the full plan output and holds it for a named human to click Approve before apply actually executes. Instead of trusting that whoever ran terraform apply on their laptop read the plan carefully, it becomes a reviewable artifact tied to a specific commit.

Terraform Cloud also supports Sentinel, HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework. A Sentinel policy runs between plan and apply and can hard-block a run outright — this example checks that every planned resource change carries an owner tag, and fails the run before a human even reaches the approval step if one is missing.

Terraform Enterprise is the same feature set — remote state, remote runs, the review UI, Sentinel, team permissions — packaged to run inside an organization's own network instead of HashiCorp's SaaS. It exists for compliance or data-residency requirements that rule out sending plan output to an external service. The real cost is operational: it's software you install, patch, and keep running yourself.

None of this is required to use Terraform well — every lesson in this course has used the CLI directly, and that remains a completely legitimate way to run it in production. Without Terraform Cloud or Enterprise, Chapter 7 shows the open-source alternative: running terraform plan inside a regular CI/CD pipeline and gating apply behind an approval step you build yourself, starting right after a deeper pass through Bicep in Chapter 6.
